## From a Plane to Three Dimensions and Independent Engines {#sec-lay-ch20}

## A Concrete Picture

A shadow puppet can reveal a hinge mechanism while hiding motion toward the
wall. A planar golf model is a carefully chosen shadow. It can expose swing-
normal force and torque mechanisms, but it cannot see out-of-plane clubface
moments, changing swing plane, or spatial joint axes.

Moving to three dimensions is not merely drawing the same links with perspective.
Finite rotations generally do not commute, moments require declared frames and
reference points, and constraints can contain new internal modes. A six-component
wrench record does not mean that every contact can exert six independent loads.

![A Planar Projection Hides Directions That a Spatial Model Must Resolve.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_planar_to_spatial.svg){#fig-lay-plane-space width=98% fig-alt="Two orange two-link sketches compare a planar projection with a spatial view containing a purple directional arrow. The schematic illustrates an omitted direction, not a measured golfer, complete wrench, or changing-axis trajectory."}

## How the Mechanism Works

In a plane, one angle and one signed moment describe each hinge. In space, body
orientation belongs to the rotation group $SO(3)$. Angular velocity is a vector,
and a moment's components depend on frame. Applying rotations in different
orders can yield different orientations.

### Spatial Wrenches Preserve the Physical Contract

A three-dimensional wrench records force $\mathbf F$ and moment $\mathbf M_O$
about a specified point $O$. For $\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OQ}$, expressing the
same loading at another point $Q$ of a rigid body gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf M_Q &= \mathbf M_O-\mathbf r\times\mathbf F,\\
\mathbf v_Q &= \mathbf v_O+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r,\\
P &= \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_O+\mathbf M_O\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\\
  &= \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v_Q+\mathbf M_Q\cdot\boldsymbol\omega.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lay-spatial-wrench-power}

All velocities here describe the same rigid motion for the **same observer**.
Rotating the components of every vector into another orthonormal basis preserves
these dot products. The wrench components themselves change. Likewise, shifting
the moment reference requires the matching change in rigid-body velocity; using
the old velocity with the new moment generally changes the reported power.

Changing the observer is a different operation. An observer translating with
constant velocity $\mathbf U$ measures $\mathbf v'_O=\mathbf v_O-\mathbf U$ and
$P'=P-\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf U$. External power and kinetic energy need not have
the same value for different observers. Rotating observers require additional
relative-motion terms in dynamics. Expressing laboratory-observed velocities in
club-aligned axes does not by itself make them club-relative velocities.

A point-force contact has no independent contact moment: its moment about $O$
is fixed by its position and force. Friction, unilateral separation, and contact
area further restrict admissible loads. A distributed grip may transmit a
resultant moment, but its six recorded components still obey the contact model.
For a deforming shaft, one rigid wrench--velocity pairing does not capture all
deformation power; sum the actual contact powers and account for internal energy.

This frame-explicit contract is the bridge from the planar negative couple to a
spatial test. The swing-normal component can be compared while additional
components reveal whether the mechanism creates undesirable twist or bending.

### Full Body Adds Redundancy

A spatial full-body model has many coordinates capable of producing similar
club motion. Inverse dynamics may estimate a net generalized-force vector for a
prescribed trajectory, but two-hand contact and muscle redundancy remain. More
coordinates do not automatically identify more biology.

The common-state spatial model therefore emphasizes action-reaction, wrench
closure, and matched interventions rather than claiming a unique human strategy.
It reports what survives and what remains open.

### Contact Closure Comes Before Contact Dynamics

A constraint Jacobian can have full row rank even when the points it would
constrain are far apart. The project tested that distinction with six
deterministic subject-scaled engineering profiles, three grip spans, and 61
prescribed states per case. The anatomical hand points miss the declared grip
points by 0.171--0.616 m, and none meets the registered 5 mm tolerance.

The same open configurations still produce a rank-six bilateral contact
Jacobian. That is not a contradiction. Rank asks whether six local correction
directions are locally available without coordinate bounds; closure asks whether
a correction is still required. Rank alone does not guarantee a finite correction
within joint limits or without collision.
Calling a rank test a contact-feasibility result would therefore hide the most
important geometric failure.

This adverse result narrowed the next model rather than weakening the scientific
program. A bounded subject-scaled solver then closed both hands on the grip while
respecting its declared joint and collision guards. It held the club at 13
prescribed samples over 0--0.24 s, while allowing pelvis, trunk, and arm coordinates
to change. All **234 of 234** profile--span--sample cases passed the **0.5 mm**
closure gate, with no stored contact error above $1.16\times10^{-10}$ m. That
numerical residual is not an anatomical measurement accuracy. A deliberately
unreachable 2.0 m grip span failed, preserving a negative control.

That success is a reduced-tree necessary condition, not proof that a person can
adopt the poses. The limits are broad engineering guards, collision clearance
uses coarse spheres, and the model omits scapular motion, forearm rotation,
multi-axis wrists, fingers, and distributed grip contact. The spatial tier still
cannot answer whether a passive mechanism reduces timing demand, creates useful
slack, improves delivery, or specifies a human technique. Subject-specific
anatomy and calibrated compliant forward contact are the next gates.

### Scapular Mobility Changes Reachability Without Identifying Strategy

The next screen makes a paired comparison within a different feasible set. It
holds the trunk and club pose fixed, then compares fixed shoulder centers
with shoulder centers that can move on a declared thoracic ellipsoid. Four
screening coordinates per side represent protraction, elevation, upward
rotation, and winging. In this surrogate, the first two move the shoulder center;
the latter two change joint orientation. This is a reduced geometry experiment,
not a validated anatomical shoulder. Its arm-only solve is not a rerun of the
234-case solve that allowed trunk motion.

The fixed branch closes **0 of 54** stored states. The mobile branch reaches
the 0.5 mm residual tolerance in **31 of 54**. The optimizer reports successful
termination in **39 of 54**, but only **16 of 54** satisfy both criteria: fifteen
closed cases lack successful termination, and twenty-three successfully
terminated cases remain open. Twenty-eight states touch a declared bound,
and an intentionally impossible 2.0 m grip span remains open. Mobility clearly
changes modeled reach, but unresolved cases may reflect range choice, omitted
coordinates, or numerical termination rather than human infeasibility.

There is a second warning. Both contact Jacobians retain rank six, while local
coordinate nullity rises from two to ten. Many scapular and glenohumeral
coordinate changes therefore leave the contact residual unchanged to first order
in the unconstrained local linearization. At an open pose this is not yet a
closed-contact manifold, and active joint bounds restrict admissible directions.
Contact geometry alone cannot tell a reviewer which internal allocation a
person used or should use.

The scientific next step is not to rename these coordinates as muscles or
coaching actions. It is to repeat the comparison with a validated articulated
shoulder, subject-specific bone geometry where governed, calibrated distributed
grip contact, and paired forward dynamics. Only then can force, work, passivity,
delivery, or human-strategy hypotheses be tested.

### Independent Engines Test Implementation Dependence

Running the same conceptual experiment in two engines tests the implementation
parts that differ, provided observables use a common convention. Report which
model construction, contact laws, derivatives, and numerical updates are shared.
Matching screenshots prove little. Matching trajectories,
wrenches, powers, constraint residuals, and negative controls is stronger.

The archived finite-mass hand-carriage experiment calls native MuJoCo
`mj_forward` and Pinocchio articulated-body forward dynamics, both version 3.8.0.
It uses a shared Kelvin--Voigt point-interface law and a shared semi-implicit
update after native acceleration evaluation. It therefore compares rigid-body
dynamics and force mapping; it does not independently test the engines' native
contact solvers or integrators. Neither branch commands the club directly.

The driver killswitch is a genuine forward intervention: starting from the same
state at 0.180 s, it removes the grounded hand-carriage driver while retaining
gravity, inertia, and interface storage and damping. In contrast, the coincident
and reversed moment-arm controls reuse achieved forces **without advancing a new trajectory**.
They test the moment calculation, not the later motion of a physically altered grip.

### Agreement Has a Boundary

If two engines agree on a reduced spatial mechanism, code-specific error becomes
less likely. Shared parameter errors, oversimplified contact, and missing anatomy
remain possible. Cross-engine agreement is verification evidence, not human
validation.

### Three-Dimensional Measurement Is Hard

Marker-based motion capture suffers soft-tissue artifact, especially around the
scapula and forearm. Joint centers and axes are estimated. Clubface orientation
requires careful rigid-body tracking. Bilateral grip sensors must be registered
to the club frame. These uncertainties should enter the model-data comparison.

**Model Result:** The archived carriage model retains a negative swing-normal
projection of its point-force moment after the driver is removed in both native
dynamics realizations. The moment-arm identities also pass their algebraic
controls. This projection is about the declared club reference; it is not an
origin-independent pure couple when net contact force is nonzero.

**Human Evidence:** Measured trunk and pelvic motion has three-dimensional
structure [@meister2011; @joyce2013]. Those kinematic studies do not test this
specific bilateral compliant-contact mechanism. McPhee reviews the broader
modeling and measurement methods [@mcphee2022]; neither that review nor agreement
between reduced models supplies participant validation for this mechanism.

**Hypothesis:** The planar swing-normal couple is one projection of a spatial
wrench pattern that should be measurable without requiring a unique muscle
allocation.

**Practical Interpretation:** A planar model can explain a shadow mechanism; a
spatial model must show which parts remain when the lights move.

### What the Plane Captures

A planar model captures rotation in one chosen swing plane and forces projected
into it. It can represent link inertia, relative release, radial/tangential
reaction, and an out-of-plane moment. Because signs and geometry are easy to
see, it is an excellent place to derive and falsify the basic negative-couple
mechanism.

The plane is not a claim that a golf swing is flat. It is a controlled slice.
Projecting a spatial trajectory is not a closed planar dynamics model: omitted
motion can alter inertia, reactions, and forces within the displayed plane.
Imposing planar constraints may itself introduce reactions absent in free space.
The key question is whether a spatial extension retains the corresponding
physical projection when out-of-plane motion and extra axes are admitted.

### What Three Dimensions Add

Each rigid body now has spatial orientation and angular velocity. The club's
moment is a vector. Hand loading can be recorded as a six-component wrench at
each declared reference, subject to the contact restrictions above.
Swing-plane normal can vary with time and must be defined operationally. Forearm
rotation, wrist deviation, shaft droop, torso side bend, and shoulder-girdle
motion introduce pathways absent from the plane.

These freedoms can redistribute a planar effect rather than merely add to it.
A moment that looked entirely negative in one axis may split across changing
axes. Preserve the complete wrench, its reference point, and the observer used
for power. A passive coordinate rotation changes components while preserving
the physical loading and scalar power; choosing a different physical projection
axis changes the reported component. The swing-normal projection remains useful
if its construction is reported and tested for sensitivity.

### Frames Must Be Registered

Laboratory, pelvis, trunk, arm, hand, club, sensor, and swing frames all move
differently. A general spatial wrench transform includes rotation and a moment
shift; either part can be trivial when axes or reference points already coincide.
Angular velocities require consistent representation; Euler-angle derivatives
are not the angular-velocity vector. These are common sources of plausible but
wrong signs.

Frame tests use known loads and orientations, action--reaction at contacts,
reference-point invariance of power, and round-trip transforms. Coordinate
conventions should be machine-readable. A reviewer should be able to reproduce
the swing-normal axis from released kinematics.

### Defining the Late Impact Zone

“Near impact” can be a clock window, a range of club position, a state-space
region, or a phase normalized between events. A spatial study should declare
the primary definition and test alternatives. If the negative-couple interval
appears only under one post hoc window, confidence is low.

State-based regions may include clubhead height, hand path, shaft orientation,
and arm--club geometry. They allow comparisons across tempo but can introduce
selection bias if tuned on outcomes. Freeze them before participant holdout.

### Independent Engines

Implement the same spatial mechanism in two dynamics engines or formulations.
Share model parameters, initial state, control histories, and output schema.
Compare trajectories, hand wrenches, constraints, energy, and the projected
couple within tolerances. Differences should be investigated, not averaged.

Independence is strongest when implementations do not share derivative code or
hidden convention helpers. Agreement then reduces the chance that one algebraic
or frame error created the result. The released comparison should include both
successful agreement and known deviations.

### A Spatial Geometry-Control Suite

These are proposed extension and measurement tests, beyond the two archived
same-force moment-arm identities. Reverse the defined swing-normal axis and verify only the reported projection
changes sign, not physical power. Swap hand positions in the model and verify
the differential couple responds. Collapse separation, align forces with the
separation vector, and rotate the swing plane. Perturb sensor-frame orientation
to quantify sign confidence.

These tests distinguish coordinate behavior from physical mechanism. If a
purported negative couple disappears whenever the reporting plane shifts a few
degrees, its interpretation should include that uncertainty rather than a binary
label. At a fixed reference point, if two unit normals differ by angle $\theta$,

$$
\left|\mathbf M\cdot(\mathbf n'-\mathbf n)\right|
\leq 2\lVert\mathbf M\rVert\sin(\theta/2).
$$ {#eq-lay-spatial-axis-bound}

A projection close to zero can reverse sign under a small angular perturbation
even when the moment vector is accurately known. For example, a moment
$(1,0,-0.01)$ N m is negative along $(0,0,1)$ but positive after that normal tilts
one degree toward the positive first axis. A sign probability additionally needs
a specified uncertainty distribution; a collection of plausible axes alone gives
a sensitivity range, not a probability.

### Moving Anatomy Without Overclaiming It

Spatial arm segments permit richer kinematics, but a ball joint at the shoulder
does not represent scapulothoracic motion or muscle recruitment automatically.
Marker-based shoulder centers and scapular orientation have substantial
measurement uncertainty. A generalized shoulder driver remains an abstraction.

The model can predict a required hand wrench or joint-level generalized load.
Mapping that to scapular retraction, protraction, or named muscle action requires
additional kinematics, physiological measurements, and a biological model.
EMG constrains activation hypotheses but does not uniquely identify muscle force.
Keeping that boundary
explicit protects the very hypothesis the work aims to test.

### Quantities That Should Survive the Extension

Whole-system energy balance for a declared observer, contact action--reaction,
consistent wrench--velocity power under passive coordinate changes,
and geometric control responses should survive exactly or within numerical
tolerance. Qualitative timing and sign of the proposed contact contribution may
survive over a declared region. Exact optimal controls and magnitudes are
expected to change.

The spatial model earns its complexity if it makes new falsifiable predictions:
out-of-plane force components, axis-dependent couple timing, or conditions under
which the planar mechanism fails. If it merely draws a more realistic golfer
while hiding the causal tests, it has moved away from science.

### Human Validation Path

Use synchronized full-body and club motion, bilateral grip wrenches, separate
force plates, and shaft deformation. Calibrate every frame and report soft-
tissue and sensor uncertainty. Evaluate participants held out from parameter
tuning. Compare predicted three-dimensional wrench trajectories, not only
clubhead speed.

Residuals should be inspected by phase and direction. A systematic out-of-plane
residual may identify missing wrist, shaft, or shoulder-girdle physics. Updating
the model in response should be declared as a new rung and retested on untouched
participants.

### Reader Lab: Rotate the World

Take one spatial state and apply one constant proper rotation to every position,
orientation, velocity, force, moment, gravity vector, and boundary/input definition.
Express inertias and constraints consistently, then recompute dynamics. This is
a passive relabeling for the same observer. The rotated trajectory and the same
scalar energy and wrench power should match. A quantity
tied to the declared swing frame should transform predictably. Failure reveals a
frame-dependent implementation error.

Next project the same contact moment onto several plausible swing-plane normals.
Report sign confidence and angular sensitivity. If all definitions agree over
the late interval, the negative-couple claim is robust to plane construction. If
they disagree, publish the dependence and prefer the complete vector result.

Finally compare two independent spatial engines on geometry-reversal and hand-
separation controls. Match initial state and input at high precision. Differences
in constraint stabilization or quaternion handling should remain below declared
observable tolerances.

### Spatial Visualization Without Illusion

A three-dimensional rendering can make a model look biologically authoritative.
Include visible joint definitions, hand contact frames, force-vector scale,
uncertainty, and model-rung label. Let readers rotate the scene and inspect the
numeric state. Do not use a detailed human mesh to imply anatomical fidelity not
present in the equations.

The best spatial figure pairs an intuitive view with declared observables: wrench
power for a named observer, projected moment with axis sensitivity, and closure residual. Beauty
should make the mechanism easier to audit, not harder to question.

### A Minimal Spatial Report

Publish body and joint frames, orientation representation, state definition,
inertias, constraints, controls, solver, and swing-plane construction. Report
complete three-dimensional hand wrenches before selected projections. Include
energy, constraint, and engine-agreement residuals. Provide geometry-control
animations with fixed vector scales and downloadable data.

For the negative couple, show the moment vector in club, laboratory, and swing
frames, the angle between vector and plane normal, and sign probability under
frame uncertainty. Report the interval by both time and state. This makes a
spatial claim reviewable rather than visually persuasive only.

### When the Planar Result Fails in Space

Failure can occur because out-of-plane motion redirects the contact wrench,
because a different axis dominates, because hand geometry changes, or because
the planar constraint created an artificial reaction. Diagnose which term
changes. A spatial failure is not proof that coupling is irrelevant; it narrows
the specific projection or validity region.

The revised explanation might say that a negative total swing-normal couple is
not robust, while one component or state-dependent regulation effect remains.
Such refinement is exactly why the model ladder exists.

### Accessibility of a Three-Dimensional Result

Pair an interactive scene with two-dimensional explanatory slices and textual
alt descriptions. A phone reader should understand hand positions, arrows, and
sign without rotating a model. A specialist can open the interactive view and
data. Providing both prevents visual sophistication from becoming an access
barrier.

### Chapter Checkpoint

The spatial extension succeeds when it preserves invariant balances, survives
frame and engine tests, and either confirms or precisely narrows the planar
mechanism. More degrees of freedom alone are not progress. New, measurable
predictions and exposed failure regions are.

For a reviewer, the full wrench vector remains primary. A convenient negative
projection should never conceal uncertainty in the axis used to define it.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The shadow analogy makes spatial extension look visually obvious. In fact,
coordinate conventions, rotation representations, and contact frames can create
subtle sign errors. Every comparison needs automated transformation and power
checks.

Engine agreement can also become false reassurance if one result is tuned to
the other. Parameters and tolerances should be registered before comparison,
with held-out cases and negative controls.
